Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-18

Summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Redwood ran through Optimize recommendations focused on batching and prefix / KV cache for Mariner Payments' customer support LLM use case. Discussed hit rates, warm vs cold cache tradeoffs, expected token reduction, and a simple cost model comparing hosted vs dedicated with KV caching enabled. Action items were to share the cost spreadsheet, sample config, and schedule a benchmark POC.

Topics:
- Workload profile and latency SLOs
- Batching strategies (per-route, dynamic batching, max latency buckets)
- Prefix caching vs full KV cache behavior and costs
- Cost model: tokens, GPU time, and expected savings
- Deployment options: hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC)
- Security/compliance notes (SOC2, KMS, audit logs)

Transcript:
[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone thanks for joining uh we gave you 45 minutes on this one to dig into Optimize recommendations for your payments assistant use case, really quick intros?
[00:08] Carlos: hey Carlos here, CTO at Mariner, I'll be walking point but Aisha and Tom are the ops leads, thanks for doing this.
[00:12] Aisha: hi all, Aisha, focused on ml infra and model ops.
[00:15] Tom: Tom, SRE, quick questions mostly around VPC and burst behaviour.
[00:18] Maya: Maya from Redwood SE, hi — I'll run through batching and cache demos and walk through the spreadsheet cost model at the end.

[00:30] Ethan: quick agenda, 1) workload profile that you sent, 2) how batching + prefix/KV cache help, 3) cost model example, 4) Q&A and next steps. if anything missing say now.

[01:02] Carlos: that sounds good. our main constraints: 95th latency under 500ms, expected peak throughput 300 rps for support chat, PII must not leave our VPC for certain customers (we have mixed residency requirements).

[01:25] Maya: ok thanks, so your trace showed median request length ~420 tokens input, response avg ~200 tokens, so roughly 620 tokens per session. are you using any multi-turn caching today?
[01:35] Aisha: no not yet; we tried an in-app LRU prefix cache but it wasn't shared across workers so hit rate was bad.

[01:43] Maya: cool so two levers we typically recommend: batching (to improve GPU utilization) and prefix/KV cache (to avoid recomputing prefixes and reduce decode tokens). batching is about throughput/cost, cache is about token reduction and latency for repeated prefixes.

[02:12] Maya: i'll start with batching — Redwood's runtime does dynamic batching with configurable max latency buckets. for example you can set latency bucket at 30ms for hot routes and 100ms for background routes. that lets you get 4-8x effective throughput on GPU for short sequences.
[02:35] Tom: does dynamic batching increase tail latency unpredictably? we can't exceed 500ms 95th.
[02:40] Maya: good question. the runtime respects route-level latency SLOs — for your support route we'd set small buckets and a max batch size tuned to hit 95th < 500ms. in practice we saw ~1.2x added decode time for batching overhead but overall latency improves under load because requests get into a larger batch. i'll show numbers in the cost model.

[03:10] Maya: moving to prefix and KV cache: prefix cache stores past KV cache snapshots for tokens up to a certain prefix length so when a prompt reuses the same lead-in we skip forward in the model, only decoding the delta. KV cache is great when you have many prompts with repeated system+user context like templates.
[03:30] Carlos: can you describe cold misses vs warm cache hit rates? what are realistic hit rates?
[03:36] Maya: sure. depends on user behavior; with templated prompts (support flows) we commonly see 40-70% prefix hit rates after some warm-up. cold-starts (new sessions) will be misses. in our spreadsheet example i show a conservative 45% hit rate and an optimistic 65% hit rate scenario.

[04:05] Maya: quick numbers: baseline (no cache, small dynamic batching) your median cost was estimated at $0.00045 per input token + $0.0009 per output token on hosted GPU pricing in our model — which is us giving a cloudy example — that yields approx $0.28 per 1000 requests given your average tokens. with KV cache at 45% hit rate we estimate token generation drops ~32% and GPU time drops ~28%, so cost per request comes down proportionally.

[04:45] Aisha: can you repeat the per-token numbers? those were approximate, i think we need them in the spreadsheet.
[04:50] Maya: yes — in the sheet: input token cost $0.00045/token (hosting estimate), decode/output $0.0009/token, model is a 13B open model, 4-bit quantized on a V100-like profile for the sample. those are placeholders to compare relative improvements; exact numbers depend on chosen instance.

[05:20] Tom: if we go dedicated, do the unit token costs change? does Redwood provide a way to estimate our committed GPU $/hr into token cost?
[05:28] Ethan: yes — Dedicated pricing converts committed $/hr and expected utilization into an effective $/token. Maya's spreadsheet has a tab where you put committed GPU $/hr and expected average concurrency and it outputs an effective $/token and per-request cost. for pilots we usually run a blended hosted->dedicated estimate so you can see break-even points.

[05:55] Maya: i'll walk the sample scenario on the spreadsheet (shared link in chat).
[06:00] Maya: Scenario A: Hosted baseline, 1M tokens/day => ~$650/day (placeholder) ; Scenario B: Hosted + KV cache (45% hit) => ~ $440/day ; Scenario C: Dedicated (reserved 1xA100 equiv) with batching + KV => ~$300/day (when utilization >60%). numbers simplified but show the direction.
[06:35] Carlos: those are meaningful. is the biggest save from reducing decode tokens or from batching GPU efficiency?
[06:40] Maya: both matter. prefix/KV cache reduces decode tokens (which are expensive per token). batching reduces idle GPU cycles and improves throughput so it reduces $/token by amortizing overhead. in our sample cache gave ~55% of the savings and batching the remaining ~45%, though results vary.

[07:05] Aisha: what about cache size and memory? we have regulatory constraints on data retention, we can't keep full conversational history forever.
[07:12] Maya: right — cache policies are configurable: TTLs, per-customer retention, and you can encrypt cache blobs with your KMS. we recommend short TTL for PII flows (e.g., 24 hours) and longer for non sensitive. Redwood Private enables cache to live in your VPC so nothing leaves your network.

[07:45] Tom: how big are cache objects? if we store prefixes up to 512 tokens and 50k unique prefixes, what memory are we looking at?
[07:52] Maya: approximate rule: KV snapshot per prefix ~ model_hidden_size * 1 byte per parameter after quantized dump — rough math: for a 13B model it's ~X MB per snapshot, but we typically store smaller horizons and compressed snapshots. in the spreadsheet i have an example: 50k prefixes at avg snapshot 0.8MB => ~40GB. that's still fine on modern SSD-backed KV store or redis+fs-backed store. we can also do partial caching (smaller prefix lengths) to cut that by 2-4x.
[08:30] Carlos: that 0.8MB/snapshot number seems high — can you share the derivation? we need it for compliance.
[08:36] Maya: yes will include derivation in the notes — it's rough but we'll give exact numbers per model size and quantization level.

[08:50] Maya: next — cache hit strategy: we do exact-match for prefixes and also support fuzzy canonicalization (strip timestamps/user ids) to increase hit rates for templated prompts. important tradeoff is canonicalization complexity vs risk of collision.

[09:10] Aisha: do you support per-tenant cache partitioning? we need to ensure tenant A can't read tenant B's cached KV snapshots.
[09:17] Maya: yes — tenant-scoped namespaces, RBAC, and you can set per-namespace KMS keys. for Private deployments we recommend dedicated namespaces.

[09:30] Ethan: quick pause — any security blockers we should address now?
[09:34] Carlos: SOC2 is required; also audit logs and SSO.
[09:37] Ethan: Redwood is SOC2 and we have SAML SSO + RBAC + audit logs; for Private we can integrate your KMS/HSM. I'll attach the security pack to the follow-up.

[09:50] Maya: back to cost math — here's a simple worked example on the shared spreadsheet:
- Baseline: 1M decode tokens/day => GPU hours = 12 ; cost = $X 
- With KV 45% hit: decode tokens = 550k/day => GPU hours = 8.6 ; cost = $Y
- With batching and 60% utilization on dedicated: effective $/token drops by ~35%

[10:20] Maya: practical recommendations for Mariner:
1) Start with hosted Optimize + KV cache enabled for the support route only (low-risk)
2) Use prefix canonicalization for templates to boost hit rate
3) Tune batching buckets for the support route to keep 95th < 500ms (we'll run benchmarks)
4) After 2 weeks of traffic, re-evaluate: if utilization > 60% move to dedicated to get better unit economics

[11:05] Carlos: pilot timeline — we want a 4-week POC with real traffic and an SLA check at the end. that aligns. what's the quickest way to get data into the model for caching?
[11:15] Maya: we recommend a 1-week warm-up with real traffic; we'll run a pre-population script that ingests your common templates and prime the prefix cache so you don't start at cold. you provide the canonical templates and logs, we run ingestion in private.

[11:35] Tom: network: we need VPC peering and private endpoints for the cache. does Redwood support VPC peering or private link?
[11:41] Ethan: yes — both; for Private we do VPC peering and for Hosted we support VPC NAT and private endpoints. we'll have infra runbooks in the security pack.

[12:00] Aisha: are there failure modes if cache store is unavailable? do we fall back to full decode gracefully?
[12:05] Maya: yes fail-open behavior: if cache unavailable we fallback to normal decode, and we can also configure degraded mode to limit concurrency to protect latency. you can also set read-through cache behavior to avoid stalls.

[12:25] Maya: quick demo — i will show two requests: one cold, one cache-hit. watch the token counts and latency.
[12:30] [screen share noise]
[12:45] Maya: cold request: 620 tokens total, time 420ms; cache-hit request: 180 tokens decoded, time 120ms. system prints show 'kv_cache_hit: true' and saved ~440 tokens.
[13:05] Carlos: nice — real numbers help. is there instrumentation to track cache hit distribution by route?
[13:10] Maya: yes — the Console shows per-route hit rate, avg saved tokens, and projected $ saved; we export daily reports to S3 or to your metrics pipeline.

[13:35] Tom: what about rolling cache invalidation for template updates?
[13:39] Maya: we support versioned cache keys; when you update templates we re-key affected prefixes so old snapshots expire quickly. we can also do TTL-based invalidation.

[14:00] Aisha: let's talk about the risk of hallucination changes after caching — if we skip early decoding, could the model produce different continuation behaviors?
[14:08] Maya: good point — prefix caching preserves the exact KV state so model continuation should be identical to having decoded the prefix live. the risk is if you canonicalize aggressively you might remove context that affects decoding; that's why we do conservative canonicalization and provide an eval harness to check for regressions.

[14:35] Maya: to mitigate quality/regression risk we integrate Redwood Optimize's evals — you provide a testset, we run before/after comparisons on outputs and surface regressions with diffs. recommended step prior to pilot.

[14:55] Carlos: okay that's critical for us. would you include the eval harness in the pilot?
[14:59] Maya: yes, included. we'll run regression tests daily during pilot.

[15:10] Ethan: quickly on pricing model for pilot — typical approach: small hosted credits + time boxed benchmarking. after success we convert to committed Dedicated if savings justify.

[15:22] Carlos: one more question: our finance team wants an estimate of break-even utilization to justify dedicated. can you show that?
[15:28] Maya: yes in the spreadsheet tab 'break-even' — with our placeholders for A100 equiv at $X/hr, break-even is around 55-65% utilization depending on hit rate. i'll send the sheet editable.

[16:00] Aisha: if we sign for Private, can we bring our own KMS and keep cache snapshots encrypted with our keys?
[16:05] Maya: yes bring-your-own-key supported, and for Private the control plane can be customer-managed. we'll include the KMS guide.

[16:20] Tom: will we get per-token latency tracing to tie to our SLO dashboards?
[16:25] Maya: yes — tracing hooks and per-request token-level timings; exports to Datadog/Prometheus.

[16:40] Ethan: ok last part — risk/concerns recap and next steps. any final technical blockers?
[16:45] Carlos: no blockers, just need the security pack and the cost sheet.
[16:48] Aisha: also will send a 7-day sample trace for warm-up.

[16:55] Ethan: great — summarize next steps: 1) Maya sends KV cache config + cost spreadsheet (by 2027-05-19), 2) Ethan sends security pack + pilot pricing (by 2027-05-20), 3) Mariner provides traffic trace and template list (by 2027-05-21), 4) schedule benchmarking week of 2027-05-24.

[17:20] Carlos: sounds good. thanks everyone.

[17:25] Maya: thanks — closing the loop, we'll post the shared links to the chat and follow up via email.

End of meeting.
